title: JP Morgan Expert Recommends 5–10-Year Bonds, Warns on Ultra-Long-Term Risks - 조선일보
content: Swa Woo highlights fiscal pressures, inflation trends, and emerging market opportunities in dollar-denominated bonds amid rate uncertainties “Current US bond yields are more attractive than they have been in recent years. However, given the possibility that long-term rates may rise further, we believe it is advantageous to focus on bonds with relatively shorter maturities, such as 5–10-year bonds, rather than long-term bonds.” Swa Woo, Asia Investment Head of Global Fixed Income at JP Morgan Asset Management, shared this perspective on US bond investment strategies on October 8. While rising bond yields and falling prices have increased the appeal of bond investments, risks remain that the US government’s fiscal deficit and increased Treasury issuance could push long-term rates higher. Woo explained, “Investors are demanding higher yields for holding long-term bonds like the 30-year US Treasury. Given the remaining room for rate hikes, caution is still needed when investing in long-term bonds.” ◇“Fiscal Spending and Corporate Investment Drive Rates Higher” Woo identified rising real interest rates as the main factor behind the 10-year US Treasury yield exceeding 5%. Real interest rates are nominal rates adjusted for inflation. He noted, “Recent government spending and corporate investment expansions have driven nominal economic growth higher than expected. Additionally, increased Treasury issuance and concerns over fiscal health have made investors more sensitive to bond investment risks.” He added, “Recent rate movements should be viewed as a structural reassessment of long-term bond values rather than just a shift in the Federal Reserve’s policy stance.” Key variables influencing future Treasury rates include wage and inflation trends, as well as government fiscal conditions. He stated, “If wage-driven inflationary pressures intensify, rates could rise further. Upcoming employment and unemployment data will be critical to watch.” Demand during Treasury auctions is also pivotal. Woo remarked, “Weak demand in auctions signals that the market is struggling to absorb the increased supply. If the US government’s fiscal situation continues to deteriorate or issuance volumes grow, investors may demand higher yields, pushing rates up.” Woo suggested that current rates already reflect many concerns, making this an attractive entry point. He said, “With rates reaching levels not seen for a long time, we see favorable buying opportunities from a long-term yield perspective. If growth or inflation indicators slow, bond prices could also rise.” However, he advised caution with ultra-long-term bonds due to their high price volatility tied to rate changes. Longer maturities amplify gains during rate cuts but also magnify losses if rates rise. Woo emphasized, “We recommend the 5–10-year maturity range but advise caution with ultra-long-term bonds. Uncertainties remain, including US fiscal policy and rising investor expectations for long-term holding yields. A gradual approach is better than aggressive investments.” The analysis also highlights emerging market bonds as a consideration. When US rates stay high and the dollar strengthens, dollar-denominated emerging market bonds may offer advantages. Woo explained, “Emerging market bonds provide higher yields to compensate for investment risks. Dollar-denominated bonds also hedge against local currency depreciation during dollar strength.” Country-wise, Brazil—with political stability and improving fiscal conditions—and India, with high economic growth, were highlighted as promising. South Korea and Taiwan also received positive assessments. Woo noted, “South Korea is benefiting from the semiconductor cycle, and its bond yield trends are attractive. Taiwan is a key beneficiary of expanded AI investments.” Among corporate bonds, he recommended those issued by major banks, which offer high credit ratings and attractive yields. He stated, “Large banks’ corporate bonds have reduced investment risks due to higher capital ratios, strengthened regulations, and solid earnings. Their additional yields over non-financial corporate bonds of the same credit rating are also appealing.”

Analyst Matt Boss raised his rating on the company to neutral from underweight. NEUTRALIZED: Shares of VF Corp. got a welcome boost on Monday, rising 5.3 percent to $15.79 after J.P. Morgan analyst Matthew Boss upgraded the stock to neutral from underweight. The upgrade wasn’t exactly a ringing endorsement, but an acknowledgment that the company is more sheltered from further downside with a “risk/reward profile” that Boss described as “more balanced.” Before the latest uptick, shares of VF were down nearly 19 percent over the past six months as the S&P 500 climbed 13.4 percent. Boss argued that much has changed at the company. VF’s top and bottom lines are on track to meet or exceed Wall Street estimates this fiscal year, he said. Helping to fuel that, the “Outdoor Anchored Portfolio” of The North Face, Timberland and Altra are targeting midsingle-digit growth in a sector projected to grow by about 6 percent for the next five years. The declines at Vans — which makes up 20 percent of VF’s business — are now “ringfenced with ‘high visibility’” for the second half, according to Boss. The fiscal 2029 margin target of 10 percent is also “on track” while net debt leverage should fall to 2.5-times in 2028 from 4.1-times in 2025. The analyst also pointed to “Portfolio Accelerators,” which are not embedded in his current forecasts, but could provide significant runway. They include the potential benefits of elevating The North Face’s image, opening more Timberland stores and shining a spotlight on Altra. Vans could also perk up with more sales to wholesalers — or even see some dealmaking. Boss pointed out that VF has a history of “evaluating M&A optionality in the portfolio” and could divest Vans as its revenues stabilize at about $2 billion after five years of declines. The analyst estimated that while a sale would cut the company’s operating income by about $40 million, it would also translate into a “$600 million capital allocation EPS break-even scenario” as money from the deal would flow into the rest of the business. title: JP Morgan: demand for iPhone 18 Pro models is stronger than for the 17 Pro models last year - GSMArena.com news - GSMArena.com
content:
Analysts are sending mixed signals – sales of the iPhone 18 Pro models in China are stronger than those of the 17 Pro models and yet Apple is reportedly cutting component orders due to weak demand. The analysts at JP Morgan are saying that there’s nothing to worry about. In a note to investors, the analysts say that the production cut is a fairly typical adjustment for Apple after a big iPhone launch. They blame it on the split launch – Apple launched the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max in September and will launch the non-Pro models early next year. The note from JP Morgan confirms the observation from China – the 18 Pro models are seeing higher demand than the 17 Pro models did last year. Not much higher, mind you, but higher. What is happening is that some people are waiting for the vanilla iPhone 18 – the vanilla model is usually the most popular one. The analysts forecast a 2% decrease in iPhone revenues because of the missing iPhone 18. Not everyone was willing to wait for it, however, which might have boosted sales of the iPhone 18 Pro. Interestingly, the 17 Pro generation is still selling strong, say the analysts, even though it’s no longer available through Apple.com. Apple has a major launch coming up – the iPhone Duo will become available next week, the company’s first foldable. JP Morgan analysts predict that it will be a hot ticket item and it will sell around 8.5 million units before the end of the year. For reference, the global shipments of foldables are expected to be between 20 and 27 million units this year. Home

title: JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs Earnings Could Move This Dow ETF—Here’s the Portfolio Math - TradingView
content: Wall Street’s earnings season kicks off Tuesday with JPMorgan Chase & Co. JPM, Goldman Sachs Group Inc. GS, Citigroup Inc. C and Wells Fargo & Co. WFC reporting results. For investors in the SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF Trust (NYSE:DIA), the first major bank reports could quickly test a portfolio exposure that is easy to overlook: nearly one-seventh of the ETF is concentrated in just two banks. DIA, which tracks the 30-stock Dow Jones Industrial Average, has 26.31% of its portfolio allocated to financials. Goldman Sachs accounted for 10.23%, making it DIA’s largest holding, while JPMorgan represented another 3.84%. Together, the two stocks made up 14.07% of the fund. The exposure reflects the Dow’s price-weighted methodology. Unlike market-cap-weighted indexes, the Dow assigns greater influence to stocks with higher nominal share prices, regardless of their companies’ total market values. That helps explain why Goldman, rather than a much larger company by market capitalization, tops DIA’s holdings. According to Investors Business Daily, FactSet forecasts the banks’s Global Banking & Markets revenue rising more than 17% to $11.86 billion, supported by investment-banking fees, advisory activity, equity underwriting and trading. However, trading trends and expenses remain key variables. Goldman CEO David Solomon said in September that non-compensation expenses could rise by more than $500 million sequentially in the third quarter, citing higher transaction costs, accelerated technology investments and charitable contributions. Moreover, management expects the fixed-income, currencies, and commodities (FICC) business to weaken in the third quarter, with Morningstar expecting a 12% sequential decline in investment banking revenue and an 11% sequential decline in FICC revenue. JPMorgan Chase presents a stronger earnings-growth outlook. Analysts expect earnings to rise 17% to $5.93 per share on revenue of $51.23 billion. Consumer and Community Banking revenue is forecast to increase 6% to $20.66 billion, while Commercial and Investment Banking revenue is expected to climb nearly 12% to $22.24 billion. Asset and Wealth Management revenue is projected to jump 24% to $7.55 billion, and net interest income is expected to rise more than 11% to $26.86 billion. For DIA, concentration creates a measurable earnings-day risk. Goldman’s results carry greater direct portfolio sensitivity. Its 10.23% weighting means a 5% move in the stock would contribute approximately 0.51 percentage points to the ETF’s return, compared with about 0.19 percentage points for the same move in JPMorgan, whose weighting is 3.84%, assuming other holdings remain unchanged. Investors will watch whether Goldman’s trading performance and cost outlook, along with JPMorgan’s lending and revenue trends, support the financial stocks underpinning the Dow-tracking ETF. The timing adds urgency. The KBW Bank Index fell 13% from its August peak and declined 6% in the third quarter, Reuters reported, despite expectations for earnings growth at major U.S. banks. Goldman’s results and guidance could carry disproportionate weight for DIA, while JPMorgan’s commentary on lending, credit quality, funding costs and investment banking could shape sentiment toward financials more broadly. Citigroup and Wells Fargo are not Dow constituents, but their results could influence the sector’s reaction. For DIA investors, Tuesday’s reports offer an early test of whether bank earnings can stabilize financial stocks, or whether disappointing guidance could turn the ETF’s concentrated exposure into a source of near-term weakness. title: JPMorgan Chase's Next Earnings Report Tomorrow Could Send the Stock Plunging. Here's Why. - The Motley Fool
content: Investors are always following JPMorgan Chase's earnings reports because the bank is a bellwether for the economy. As it does each quarter, JPMorgan Chase (JPM +0.39%), the largest bank in the U.S., will kick off earnings season tomorrow morning by releasing its third-quarter results before the market opens. Then management, led by CEO Jamie Dimon, will host a live conference call with analysts. Investors across the market are always interested in what the big banks, particularly JPMorgan, have to say because they serve as a pulse check on the economy, showing how consumers and businesses are holding up. Bank stocks have also come under pressure amid soaring bond yields, which can affect banks in various ways. Here's why JPMorgan's earnings report tomorrow could send the stock plunging. Rising bond yields have taken their toll on the stock market, and the big banks have not been spared. Banks are a very interest-rate-sensitive business, so it makes sense. Bond yields increase banks' funding costs and raise the cost of capital in the capital markets, which can slow investment banking activity. They can also slow lending activity by making borrowing more expensive. When the Total Conviction signal flashed for Nvidia in 2009, most people ignored it. The ones who acted turned $5,000 into $3,105,454*. Now, for the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. It’s a key player in the $1.8 trillion space race, and with the stock recently sitting 20% off its highs, the window to get in early is closing fast. While bond yields will also increase interest income, potentially boosting revenue in bank loan portfolios, they can also put pressure on borrowers with adjustable-rate loans and those refinancing. That's why bank credit will come into focus. It's been benign for a very long time now, and higher yields will make investors more nervous about a credit cycle. Still, the full effects of rising bond yields may not be felt just yet, and JPMorgan largely expects a robust third quarter for investment banking and trading. During a conference on Sept. 15, JPMorgan Chase Co-President Doug Petno said the bank expects investment banking fees and markets revenue ​to grow in the "mid-to-high teens" percentage range in the third quarter. In the second quarter, these businesses posted blistering numbers with investment banking fees up 30% year over year and 14% from the previous quarter. Markets' revenue, which can be influenced by trading activity, blasted 35% higher year over year. That's a tough comparison, especially for investment banking, which had its best quarter since 2021. Major initial public offerings, such as Space Exploration Technologies Corp, contributed to the banner second quarter. Still, if Pento's guide comes to fruition, that would still be very solid. "We ⁠started this quarter with a strong pipeline that continues. I touched on management and board confidence-that's ​driving tremendous amount of M&A activity. It's as high as we've seen in some time," he said during the September conference. Although rising bond yields have been somewhat priced in over the past month, they could still pressure parts of JPMorgan’s business, and I think investors will be very cautious about any signs of weakness. Wall Street analysts, on average, expect the bank to report $5.94 in adjusted earnings per share on revenue of $51.22 billion. Furthermore, management last quarter guided for full-year net interest income of $105.5 billion, including market revenue. Adjusted expenses are projected at $107.5 billion. Investors may sell the stock if the bank fails to beat estimates or uphold its full-year guidance. Ultimately, I do feel that investors have a high bar heading into earnings, and more could go wrong than right. For instance, while Pento gave solid investment banking and markets guidance, it still has a tough comparison to the second quarter, and there have been rumblings that investment banking and trading activity is set to slow. While the economy has been resilient, investors have been anticipating a credit cycle for some time, so any signs of deteriorating credit quality could trigger a sell-off. I don’t necessarily expect the quarter to be a disaster, but the slightest miss or any signs of concern could lead the market to press the sell button. While bond yields will also increase interest income, potentially boosting revenue in bank loan portfolios, they can also put pressure on borrowers with adjustable-rate loans and those refinancing. That's why bank credit will come into focus. It's been benign for a very long time now, and higher yields will make investors more nervous about a credit cycle. Still, the full effects of rising bond yields may not be felt just yet, and JPMorgan largely expects a robust third quarter for investment banking and trading. During a conference on Sept. 15, JPMorgan Chase Co-President Doug Petno said the bank expects investment banking fees and markets revenue ​to grow in the "mid-to-high teens" percentage range in the third quarter. In the second quarter, these businesses posted blistering numbers with investment banking fees up 30% year over year and 14% from the previous quarter. Markets' revenue, which can be influenced by trading activity, blasted 35% higher year over year. That's a tough comparison, especially for investment banking, which had its best quarter since 2021. Major initial public offerings, such as Space Exploration Technologies Corp, contributed to the banner second quarter. Still, if Pento's guide comes to fruition, that would still be very solid. "We ⁠started this quarter with a strong pipeline that continues. I touched on management and board confidence-that's ​driving tremendous amount of M&A activity. It's as high as we've seen in some time," he said during the September conference. Although rising bond yields have been somewhat priced in over the past month, they could still pressure parts of JPMorgan's business, and I think investors will be very cautious about any signs of weakness. Wall Street analysts, on average, expect the bank to report $5.94 in adjusted earnings per share on revenue of $51.22 billion. Furthermore, management last quarter guided for full-year net interest income of $105.5 billion, including market revenue. Adjusted expenses are projected at $107.5 billion. Investors may sell the stock if the bank fails to beat estimates or uphold its full-year guidance. Ultimately, I do feel that investors have a high bar heading into earnings, and more could go wrong than right. For instance, while Pento gave solid investment banking and markets guidance, it still has a tough comparison to the second quarter, and there have been rumblings that investment banking and trading activity is set to slow. While the economy has been resilient, investors have been anticipating a credit cycle for some time, so any signs of deteriorating credit quality could trigger a sell-off. I don't necessarily expect the quarter to be a disaster, but the slightest miss or any signs of concern could lead the market to press the sell button. JPMorgan Asset Management plans to lift its European assets under management to $2tn over the coming five years, doubling its current regional total, reported the Financial Times citing a company official. "That's an expensive commitment but we think it's necessary," he added. The company has avoided corporate takeovers to fuel expansion. Ahead of the inaugural budget under Prime Minister Andy Burnham's government later this month, Thomson indicated a positive stance on Britain's economic trajectory. title: What To Expect From JPMorgan Chase’s (JPM) Q3 Earnings - TradingView

It was a strong quarter for the company, with a narrow beat of analysts’ tangible book value per share and EPS estimates. Is JPMorgan Chase a buy or sell going into earnings? Read our full analysis here, it’s free for active Edge members. Analysts covering the company have generally reconfirmed their estimates over the last 30 days, suggesting they anticipate the business will stay the course heading into earnings. JPMorgan Chase has a history of exceeding Wall Street’s expectations.
